s04.slug: MONDAY · 11:52 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL, THE 3RD–4TH LANDING
body: The bulb on the landing lives in a wire cage, and it makes a cage of the light too: a grid of shadow thrown down the concrete steps and up the cinderblock, with Jack sitting in the middle of it on the third step from the top, in his socks. Behind him, up half a flight and down the hall, 412 is dark and Theo is asleep in it, with Hollis in his teacup on the nightstand keeping the watch. Jack opened the landing window when he came out. It goes six inches and no further, and the night comes in through the gap, eucalyptus and wet asphalt and a fine rain that hasn’t made up its mind, ticking now and again on the sill.

He came out here at half past eleven because 412 is too small for a phone that lights up. He knows what it looks like, a man taking his phone into a stairwell at midnight. It’s been two nights. Marisol has been a very large town for two nights, and he has the RAZR in both hands between his knees, shut, like something he’s keeping warm.
It goes, and goes again, and again — three texts crawling in one behind the other on the RAZR’s little screen, a line at a time.

body.text: took this at 1. sat on it 11 hours
the wedding episode. im not the bride. i checked
3 of me and not one of them knows what youre going to say

body: Then the little screen says *New Picture Msg*, and then nothing, for so long that he looks up at the bulb. The RAZR takes its time with pictures. It drinks them through a straw. When this one comes it arrives as a gray stamp in the corner of the screen, a square of pale shapes the size of a postage stamp that won’t hold still, and he tilts it toward the cage of light until the grain settles. He doesn’t open it. The three lines sit over it like a cover letter.

The others have come as if she couldn’t wait. This one waited. She took it at one in the afternoon and carried it around Burbank all day, through whatever a fitting is and whatever comes after a fitting, and at eight minutes to midnight she decided. His thumb is on the button.

choices.key: You opened the picture she sat on for eleven hours, and told her yes.
response: He opens it.

A fitting room: he works that out first, from the pins. A three-way mirror, the tall kind, with a row of pins stuck in the frame of the middle panel and the end of a rolling rack hung with garment bags. She’s standing in the middle of it with the white phone held low at her hip, and the two side panels have taken her and turned her, so that she’s there three times at once — once facing him, once from each side — and in the left-hand glass is the long line of her back, nape to heel, which no picture has ever given him, because she has always been the one holding the camera.

And the dress is coming off. Not off: coming off, caught on its way down — pale silk, not white, slipped from her shoulders and fallen nearly the whole way, pooled at her ankles, one bare foot lifted to step out of it. Every picture she has sent him she has held still for. In this one she’s moving. He can practically hear the silk go.

Her chin is level. Her mouth is open a little, the way a mouth is when it was about to say something and stopped to hear what you’d say first. She’s asking. In a room in Burbank with the door unlocked and somebody gone down the hall for pins — five minutes, at most — she took a picture of herself asking him a question, and then she carried it eleven hours to see if she still wanted to ask.
He sits on the step with the phone close to his face and wants her so badly, so exactly, that it puts him back against the cinderblock. He doesn’t look away from it. He answers it.

response.text: you looked like you were asking me something. yes
ok. good. that was the right answer

response: Out on the sill the rain makes up its mind. It comes all at once, heavy, the first real rain of the week, loud on the glass and blowing in through the gap in a cold fine spray across the landing, over his socks and his knees and the shut phone in his hand, and he sits in it and lets it.

choices.key: You left her picture unopened until you could see her face.
response: He takes his thumb off the button.

The square stays a gray square at the bottom of the menu, eleven hours old and getting older. Whatever she was asking him at one o’clock this afternoon, in whatever room in Burbank, she can ask him with her face. He’d rather have the face. He has wanted to see her face for two days more than he has wanted almost anything, and a picture of it the size of a stamp, under a cage, at midnight, is the wrong size.
He answers the captions instead, one key at a time.

response.text: im not opening it till i can see your face. wednesday
wednesday then. ill watch you open it. youll hate it

response: He has a feeling he won’t hate it at all.

Out the window the rain stops thinking about it. It comes down all at once, the first real rain of the week, drumming on the sill and coming in through the gap in a cold spray that beads on his socks, and he sits on the step with the shut phone against his mouth, and doesn’t get up to close the window.

choices.key: You opened her picture, looked once, and erased it.
response: He opens it, and looks once.

A fitting room, a three-way mirror, three of her — front and both sides, the long line of her back in the left-hand glass — and pale silk fallen to her ankles with one bare foot stepping out of it, and her face, chin level, mouth just open, asking him something and waiting to hear.

He holds the button down. The RAZR asks him if he’s sure. He is. *Erased.* The square is gone and the menu closes up over the place where it was, and the question isn’t gone at all. He can still see the foot. He can still see her chin. He has the one look, and that’s all he’s going to have, and he can tell already it’s going to be plenty.
He looks at the two question marks. There’s nothing he can put under them that’s true and that he can send. He closes the phone.

The rain has made up its mind while he was making up his. It’s coming hard now on the window, the first real rain of the week, and it blows in through the gap onto the landing and onto his socks, and he stays where he is on the step with the shut phone on his knee.

body: Thursday the south wall of Morro 1100 was full of sun. Today it’s a sheet of gray with water going down it, floor to ceiling, shuddering a little in the gusts, and what comes through it is the light at the bottom of a pool. A third of the hall has stayed in bed. The rest have brought the storm in with them on their shoes.

Up in the back row the corner seat under the exit sign is empty, with nothing on it. No book keeping a place; no hood; no feet up on the seat in front. It’s folded up. Jack takes the seat beside it and puts *Oceanography 1* on his own knees.

Fenner comes on at eleven in the Tevas — in January, in this — with the coffee, and because of the third that stayed home he takes roll by pairs, off a sheet, not looking up. “Thirty-nine. Forty. Forty-one.”
“Half,” Jack says.
Fenner looks up at the back row over the coffee, at the folded seat and the one beside it.
“She says to tell you she’s drowning in Beverly Hills.”
“Not for drowning,” says Fenner, and makes his mark, and calls forty-two.

body.text: It’s exactly how she said he’d say it, Thursday, in his own Texas, and Jack has to look down at his book.

body: Two rows down a girl in a crew sweatshirt brings her phone up at the angle that’s meant to look like checking the time, and points it at the back row. At the corner seat. The phone goes down.
Fenner does tides. Ten minutes into them the RAZR goes in Jack’s pocket, and he opens it under the lip of the fold-down desk.

body: With eight minutes of tides to go, every phone in the hall goes off at once.

body.text: SEVERE WEATHER: Stay indoors. Avoid creek paths and low-lying areas. Updates at alert.marisol.edu

body: It’s a sound he has never heard in one room: two hundred phones going together, buzzing in pockets and backpacks and on the fold-down desks, chirping, a ringtone down front playing four bright bars of something and stopping. All over the hall the screens light up in the gray, row after row of them, until the room is full of little lit faces looking down into their laps. Fenner stops talking. He stands at the whiteboard with the dying marker in his hand and looks past all of them, up at the glass, where the rain has gone flat sideways and the eucalyptus on the hill are bent over like they’re listening for something.

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 6:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE → THE HARBOR, IN THE RAIN
body: The TV is the only light on in the fourth-floor lounge, and it throws a cold blue onto the windows, where the rain is coming down them in sheets and taking the blue with it. The cable is back. On the door, under Priya’s SEVERE WEATHER PROTOCOL, a second laminate has gone up since four o’clock: CABLE RESTORED. YOU’RE WELCOME.
Jack stands in the doorway with his Anchor shirt over his arm and his hair wet from the shower, and reads the two texts he didn’t answer.

body.text: are you in a basement. tomas says everyone in las olas is in a basement
hello??

body: At 4:31 he was in the laundry room. At 4:47 he was on the stairs.

On the screen a map of Massachusetts has gone red from the outside in, and a man at a glass desk is using the word *stunning* for what has to be the fourth time. They’ve called it. A Republican state senator from a town called Wrentham, a guy nobody in the lounge had heard of at Christmas, has taken Ted Kennedy’s seat, fifty-two to forty-seven, and the man at the desk keeps saying *Kennedy’s seat* the way you’d say a church burned down.

Doug is on the floor in front of the set in his sleeping bag. “My cousin in Worcester called it,” he tells the room. “Like, in November. He has a lot of opinions. He has a truck. He says it’s all the truck.”
Kevin, on the arm of the couch, thumbing his BlackBerry: “They’re saying forty-one. He’s the forty-first vote.”
“Of what?” says Doug.
“Of no.”
Margot is in the armchair with her Docs up on the coffee table. “A filibuster-proof majority,” she says, “that lasted from a swearing-in to a special election. I’d like that on a sampler.”
The man on the screen says *Kennedy* again. It’s six past six. Jack is due at the Anchor at seven.
Eight minutes later he’s in the bus shelter on Ocean Road, with the rain blowing in under the roof at his shins, and he calls her back.
“Massachusetts,” Skye says. “Go.”

She’s out. He can hear it: a corridor somewhere with a vending machine in it, a door with a pneumatic sigh, and her voice half a step up and racing on whatever she has been drinking out of paper cups since ten this morning. “I’ve been in a booth for seven hours breathing at myself, and the sound guy had CNN on his laptop with the sound off the whole afternoon, and everybody in that building looks like their dog died, and I need somebody to explain to me why. Go.”
He starts. He gets to the sixty votes.
“Wait. Are you walking?”
“I’m at a bus stop.”

“Walk.” A machine clunks something into a tray on her end. “I can hear you standing. You’re standing in a little glass box like a bus-stop Republican. New rule: you explain your politics while you walk, and I tell you why you’re wrong, and at the end you’ve had exercise.”
“Since when is that a rule?”
“Since now. I’ve been told when to breathe all day. I’m making rules.” A paper cup crunches. “Call me back when you’re walking.”
And she hangs up on him.
He rides the 11 to the harbor with the phone in his fist and the bus windows streaming, and gets off at the foot of the wharf, and puts his hood up, and calls her back.
“I’m walking.”
“I can hear it. You squelch. Go.”

So he walks the wharf, out toward the end of it with the RAZR inside his hood against his ear, past the bait shack and the shut fish market and the boats knocking in their slips, and he explains Massachusetts.

Ted Kennedy had that seat for forty-seven years. Since he died in August a friend of his has been keeping it warm, and it’s been one of the sixty — the number you need in the Senate to stop the other side talking a bill to death — and on Christmas Eve the health-care bill went through the Senate with sixty exactly, not one to spare. As of tonight it’s fifty-nine. Brown is the forty-first no.
“So you’re happy,” Skye says.
“I’m glad the bill’s in trouble. I’m not glad about him.”
“Explain the difference. Walk faster, you slow down when it gets complicated.”

He walks faster. The bill, the way the Senate wrote it, pays for abortion — not straight out; there’s a deal in it Ben Nelson got that’s supposed to wall the money off, and the bishops say the wall’s made of paper. The House passed a real wall, the Stupak amendment, and now the two bills have to become one bill, and he would rather have no bill than the Senate’s. “That part I’m glad about.”
“And the man.”

“The man’s pro-choice. Sort of. The Massachusetts kind.” A gull goes up off a piling in front of him, complaining. “And Massachusetts already has its own health care, basically everybody covered — Romney’s — and Brown voted for it. So the guy who’s going to stop the national one voted for the state one, and he’s pro-choice, and he won driving around in a truck. I’m not getting the bumper sticker.”
“You don’t have a bumper. You have a bus pass.”
“I have a very nice bus pass.”

“Okay. My turn.” She’s walking too; he can hear heels on concrete, the big hollow echo of a parking structure. “Massachusetts didn’t vote against health care, Jack. You just told me — they have health care. They voted against being taken for granted. She ran like she’d already won. She called the baseball guy a Yankees fan.”
“Curt Schilling.”

“I don’t know who that is and I’m offended on his behalf.” A car door, a long way off in the garage, booms. “And the people who write the checks for those ads didn’t think they had to show up for this one. I know those people. I’ve been to their houses. They have a lot of art about the poor.”
He laughs. She doesn’t give him time to recover.
“And he posed *nude*. In *Cosmo*.”
“He posed nude in *Cosmo* and won a Senate seat,” Skye says. “I posted a surfboard and I’m on probation.”

He laughs so loud, out there on the wharf in the rain, that a man hosing down a fish-cleaning table under a work light looks up from it. She laughs with him, and then, not quite laughing: “I mean it. Corinne sent me an email with a *subject line*.”
“What was the subject line?”
“*Going forward*. In italics.” A door hisses on her end. “Oh — and Tomás texted. Your tornado went down Del Playa. It took Sol’s swing.”
“Took it?”
“*Took* it. Like Oz. Sol’s devastated. She’s been sitting on the steps all afternoon in mourning. Tomás found one of the chains in the neighbor’s yard.” The heels stop. “It was a good swing.”
He’s at the end of the wharf by then, at the rail, with the harbor black and jumping under the lights and the rain coming across it in curtains. The left chain squeaked every time it went back.
“It was a good swing,” he says.

He turns around and starts back up the wharf, because it’s twenty to seven, and because she isn’t finished, and because he isn’t either. Somewhere in a parking garage in Burbank she’s walking in circles so she can keep arguing, and he is soaked to the knees on a wharf in a storm doing the same, and he could not tell you one thing that’s wrong.

choices.text: “They didn’t vote for him. They voted against being told.”
choices.key: Walking the wharf in the storm, you told Skye Massachusetts voted against being told.
response: “That’s *mine*,” Skye says. “That’s what I said.”
“You said it worse.”

“I said it *first*.” She gives him nothing; she laughs at him instead, the whole length of the bait shack, and makes him say it again so she can tell him what’s wrong with it, which is that it’s hers.

By the time he gets to the Anchor’s back door he’s wet through to the skin, the Carhartt dark to the elbows, the shirt over his arm wet under it, his sneakers full, and he’s still losing and can’t stop laughing at the water pouring off the eave. “I have to go wash dishes.”
“Say goodbye like a senator.”

He does it in the voice of every man who ever stood at a podium in a blue tie — he thanks the good people of the Commonwealth, he thanks his wife and his truck — and she shrieks in the parking garage, and hangs up on him for the second time tonight.

choices.text: “You’re right about Massachusetts. It already had its own.”
choices.key: Walking the wharf in the storm, you gave Skye Massachusetts: it already had its own health care.
response: There’s a silence on her end, in the garage, long enough that he takes the phone away from his ear to see if he’s lost her. He hasn’t. It’s her being pleased.
“Say it again at the next pier,” she says.

He says it again at the next pier, and at the next one, because she asks, all the way back up the wharf in the rain past the bait shack and the fish market, until he’s standing at the Anchor’s back door wet to the skin, with water coming off the eave onto his hood, laughing too hard to say it right.
“Goodbye like a senator.”
“I yield the remainder of my time,” Jack says.
“*Motion carried*,” says Skye, and she’s gone.

choices.key: Walking the wharf in the storm, you told Skye *Cosmo*’s a magazine and she’s a Facebook.
response: “I’m a *Facebook*?” She’s delighted. He can hear the heels start up again. “I’m going to put that on my headstone. Under the other thing. *Beloved daughter. Also a Facebook.*”
“You can’t argue with it.”

“I can argue with anything, I’m from Los Angeles.” And she does, all the way back up the wharf: that a magazine is a Facebook with staples, that the centerfold was 1982 and she was 2010 and that’s worse for *him*, that he’s only winning because he’s outside.
He gets to the Anchor’s back door wet through to the skin, under the drip off the eave, and has to lean on the dumpster lid to finish laughing. “I have to go wash dishes.”
“Goodbye like a senator.”
“The gentleman from Ohio has to go wash dishes.”

“The gentleman from Ohio is *excused*,” Skye says, and she’s gone, and he stands under the eave a little longer with the phone against his chest and the rain coming off the gutter in a rope in front of him.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE CURB → MARISOL POINT, THE DIRT LOT → THE BLUFF ROAD
s12.music: Empire of the Sun — “Walking on a Dream”

body.text: outside. top down. dont bring an umbrella

body: It has been raining on Delgado since Monday night, steadily, with conviction, and the Saab is at the curb in it with the top down. The seats are dark with water. There’s water standing in the cupholders. Skye is behind the wheel in a soaked gray hoodie with the hood back and sunglasses on — sunglasses, at twenty to five on a January afternoon in a storm — and she’s laughing at him before he’s through the door.

She drove up the 101 from Burbank with the top up as far as the Rincon, she tells him later, and put it down there for the last ten miles because she missed weather. Los Angeles doesn’t have weather. Los Angeles has a forecast.

He makes it to the curb. She’s out of the car and around the hood before he can get to the door of it, and she takes his face in her two wet hands and kisses him on the sidewalk in front of Delgado Hall, in the rain, under every window on that side of the building, long enough that the rain gets into it — into his collar, into the corners of her mouth — and she laughs into it and keeps going.
“Three nights,” she says, when she’s done. “You look like you’ve been in a basement.”
“I was.”
“Tomás said.” She digs in the pocket of the hoodie.

body.text: She comes out with two mints, wrapped, warm from her. “As ordered.” One of them has a bite out of the corner of the wrapper. That one, she explains, was on the network man’s bread plate, beside his roll, and she took it while he was telling her about her brand, and held his eye, and the bite is where she had to get it open with her teeth under the table because she needed both hands to look interested.

She comes out with one mint, off a pillow somebody important was going to sleep on, and presents it to him on her flat palm in the rain like a ring. “It guarded your shirt,” she says. “It never left its post.”

body: Then she peels the hoodie off over her head right there on the sidewalk, and under it is his flannel, and she peels that off too and hands it to him, wet on the outside and warm on the inside and smelling of a hotel — some soap he couldn’t afford the name of. “It hated it,” she says. “It sat in a parking garage and thought about you. *Avatar* won everything. Everybody told me they saw it in 3-D. A man who owns part of a *studio* told me he saw it in 3-D like he was telling me he’d been to Lourdes.”

body.text: “Now,” she says. “Open it.” She means here, now, on the curb in the rain. “I want to see what you think. I didn’t know what you’d think.” So he gets the RAZR out under the flannel and opens it — three of her, the size of a stamp, with rain beading on the screen — and she doesn’t look at the phone once. She watches his face. Whatever his face does, she sees it before he has a word ready — he watches her see it — and he puts the phone in his pocket, and she takes hold of the front of his shirt for a second, hard.

“‘I saw it,’” she quotes at him. “Period. Like a receipt.” “I saw it,” he says. She looks at him through the rain running down her sunglasses, and whatever she’s deciding about that, she keeps. She takes his hand instead, and pulls him toward the car.
“You said yes,” she says. “I said yes.” She pushes the sunglasses up into her wet hair to watch him say it again, so he says it again, and she looks pleased enough to be dangerous.

body: “Get in,” she says. “We need field data.”

She takes Seacliff out to the end of it with the top down and the wipers going for no reason, since most of the rain is coming in over the top of the windshield. The dirt lot at the end of Seacliff is a brown lake with a sawhorse across the mouth of it and a county sign zip-tied to the sawhorse — BEACH CLOSED · NO WATER CONTACT — and she noses the Saab up to the sawhorse and kills the engine, and they sit in the open car in the rain in the last of the light, and look.

The Point isn’t there. Not the Point he’s seen from this lot, with the long lines walking in out of the west and bending at the reef the way she drew them on his legal pad, peeling off it one after another, neat as a zipper. There aren’t any lines. The sea is brown a mile out, and from the reef to the sand it’s white, all of it, standing up and falling over in every direction at once, and the noise of it comes up the bluff and into the car and doesn’t stop for breath.
“The reef’s still aiming it,” Jack says. “Everything at the same rocks. It’s just all arriving at once.”
Skye has her chin on the top of the door, her wet hair stuck to her cheek. “It’s not breaking where it does,” she says. “It’s breaking everywhere.”

Up the bluff from the lot the old Light stands white and shut, and below it the low wall runs along the edge, and at the end of the wall is the white cross. Somebody leaves flowers there on Sundays — Tomás said so — and Sunday’s are gone, torn off by yesterday’s wind. All that’s left at the foot of the cross is a length of red ribbon snagged on the fence wire, standing straight out sideways in the gale.
“Somebody’s going to be sad Sunday,” Skye says.
Jack looks up at the crossbar, at the name he knows there, with the rain running down the white paint over it.
She starts the car.

The bluff road runs north along the top of everything, and she takes it with the top down in the downpour, and puts her iPod on the dash and turns it up as far as the Saab goes — something big and bright and synthesized, a song built for driving fast in the sun — and they drive it in the rain. The heater’s on full, roaring at their shins, cooking their ankles while the rest of them drowns. He doesn’t know the words. He screams it anyway, whatever the words are, and so does she, with the rain coming straight down into the car and into their open mouths, and the eucalyptus going by black and streaming on the right, and on the left the sea white out to the edge of what they can see. She drives with one hand and puts the other up into the rain, palm open, catching it. Her hair is plastered flat. Her mascara is a ruin. She has never looked better and she would kill him for saying so, and he says so, at the top of his lungs, over the song, and she screams with laughter and doesn’t take her hand down.

At a turnout above the water she pulls off and stops, and turns the music down, and leaves the engine running with the heater going. The rain comes down on them. Her thumb is going on the wheel, back and forth, one small stroke.

“Tuesday,” she says, “you didn’t answer me for an hour and forty-three minutes. I counted. And then you called me from a bus shelter and you were funnier than you’ve ever been in your life.” She’s looking at the water, not at him. “You were *so* funny, Jack.”
He doesn’t say anything.
“Something happened Tuesday that isn’t the tornado.”

The rain on the hood. The heater. He doesn’t answer her, and she doesn’t make him; she lets it be. Her thumb stops on the wheel. She reaches over and wipes the rain off his eyebrow with it, the left one, across the scar, and then she leans over him and gets the white phone out of the glove box, where it has been staying dry.

She reaches up and clicks on the little map light over the mirror, and holds the phone out at arm’s length with its back to them, because that’s the only way, and leans in against him, wet from her hair to her shoes, and takes it. Takes three. She shades the screen with her hand and looks, and turns it around to show him the one she wants: the two of them in an open car in a storm in the dark, grainy, lit gold from above, her hair stuck to her head and her mouth wide open laughing at the lens, and him turned toward her instead of it, laughing too, with rain in his mouth. The drops show up in the light as white streaks, falling through the whole picture. It doesn’t look like January. It looks like two people who haven’t heard about January.
“Can I?” she says.

journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Till May. No trades. Thursday: partners by seat. Skye, till May. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown. Tuesday: half of Pair 41. Wednesday: field data from the lot in a storm — it wasn’t breaking where it does. It was breaking everywhere.

response: She’s typing before he’s done saying it, thumbs fast on the wet glass, the tip of her tongue in the corner of her mouth. “Corinne said nothing new goes up till she says,” she says, not looking up. “Corinne’s had three days. Corinne should’ve said.”

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:20 PM · THE SAAB, SEACLIFF ROAD
body: The top is up at last; it went up at the light at Seacliff and Ocean with the motor whining. With it up the Saab is a small loud room — rain drumming on the canvas a foot over their heads, the wipers going, the heater going, the two of them steaming in it like laundry. Her hair is in wet ropes. His jeans are a different color than they were this morning.
Skye has been up since four, in Studio City. She tells him so with her head back on the headrest and her eyes shut, at a red light, with her hand on the gearshift.

“Come home with me,” she says. “I’ll make you cereal.” She rolls her head on the headrest to look at him. “I had plans for you. I had a *list*. And my body vetoed them. My body has filed a formal objection, and it’s going to be asleep by nine whether I like it or not.”
He has three pages due on Hale’s table at one o’clock tomorrow, and he hasn’t written a word of them.
The light goes green. She doesn’t go. She waits, with her hand on the shift, for him.

choices.cue: Skye will hold on to that.
choices.key: Wednesday night you went home with Skye, and she fell asleep in the middle of a sentence.
response: She puts the car in gear before he’s finished saying yes, and goes through the green that’s already gone yellow, and takes the turn for Las Olas one-handed, with the other hand on his knee in case he thinks about getting out.

choices.key: Wednesday night you took Skye to Giorgio’s and wrote your pages while she read you waves.
response: “I love watching people work,” she says, and puts it in gear. “It’s my favorite thing nobody pays me for.”
She swings them back toward Mission Street with the wipers on high, and at the next light she leans over and steals the flannel back off his knee.

s12b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:10 PM · DEL PLAYA, THE HOUSE
body: The porch smells of Sol’s cigarette and wet boards. Sol is on the top step under the eave in a man’s raincoat three sizes too big, with her knees up and her old camera in her lap, smoking like a widow. She doesn’t get up. She lifts the cigarette at Skye, and at Jack, and puts it back in her mouth.

Over her head, in the porch ceiling, there are two hooks with nothing on them. A length of chain still hangs from the left one, swaying in the wind off the water, tapping the post. The other chain is lying on the boards by the door in a wet coil where Tomás dropped it, the last link at the end of it pulled open. Where the swing went is anybody’s guess. The ocean, Tomás thinks.
Skye crouches on the step beside Sol and puts her arm around the raincoat. “We’ll get another swing.”
“There isn’t another swing,” says Sol.

The screen door bangs and Tomás puts his head out — wet hair, board shorts in January, a mixing bowl of something in one hand. He looks at the rain. He looks at Jack. “Point’s closed, bro,” he says, and takes his bowl back inside.

body.text: Osei said sit on her porch. There’s nothing on the porch to sit on.

body: Her room is cold, and the window over the mattress is black with the water somewhere down below it. She takes the wet flannel off him and hangs it over the heater, and makes cereal for dinner in two mixing bowls, because every bowl in the house is in the sink — Honey Nut Cheerios, with the last of Tomás’s milk — and they eat it sitting on her mattress with their backs against the wall, in dry sweats she finds for both of them, his too short in the leg. When the flannel is warm she puts it on over her T-shirt and pulls the cuffs down over her hands, and lies down across the mattress with her head in his lap.
His hand goes into her hair. It’s still damp at the roots, cold, and it smells like rain and somebody else’s shampoo.

She tells him the party. She does the man from the network — a tan like a good saddle, calls everybody *kid*, asked her four separate times whether she’d been thinking about her *brand* — and then she does the ficus, which is mostly a long and dignified silence with leaves in it, and which she says was the better conversationalist by a mile. She does Corinne two tables over mouthing *smile* at her across the ballroom, all teeth, like a woman warning somebody off a ledge. She does the bathroom: a woman in a gown on the phone to her mother in Encino, crying about a seating chart; two girls from a show she won’t name being very busy in the end stall; and her on the closed lid with her shoes off, the only one in there not working.

“And you texted me about rain,” she says. She tips her head back in his lap to look up at him upside down. “Everybody in that hotel was talking about *Avatar*, and you sent me the weather in Marisol. I read it in the car on the way home. Twice.”
Her eyes close. The heater ticks.
“Friday,” she says. “Conan’s last show. Here. On Tomás’s TV. I’m going to be awake for it. I am going to be so awake, Jack. I’m going to make popcorn and be sad about a man I’ve never met.”
“I’ll be here.”

“Good.” Her hand finds his knee through the flannel cuff and stays there. She’s on Corinne again by twenty to ten — Corinne’s email, Corinne’s subject line, how Corinne writes *per our conversation* about conversations that never happened — and she’s halfway into “and then she copied my *mother* on it, which is —” when the sentence just stops. He looks down. Her mouth is a little open and her breath has gone long and slow, and her hand has gone loose on his knee. Nine-forty, by the clock on her dresser, and she’s out, in the middle of a sentence about Corinne.

response: He gets the blanket off the foot of the mattress without moving his knee, and brings it up over her to the chin. Then he works himself out from under her head, a little at a time, and puts the pillow where his lap was. She doesn’t wake. She pulls the blanket in under her chin with the cuff of his flannel and says something to the pillow that isn’t a word.

At a quarter to eleven Tomás drives him back to campus in the van, with two boards loose in the back rattling over every pothole on Del Playa and the wipers losing. Tomás doesn’t say a thing the length of Las Olas. At the Delgado curb he leans on the wheel and looks up through the windshield at the rain, and says his second sentence of the night, which is the same as his first. “Point’s closed, bro.”

choices.text: *Leave a note on her Oceanography book.*
response: Her pencil is in the gutter of *Oceanography 1*, on the floor by the mattress, where she’s been keeping the place at chapter four. He gets it without moving his knee and writes on the cover, small, in the corner where she’ll see it first.

response.title: On the cover of *Oceanography 1*, in pencil
response.text: pages. tomorrow. you snore like a senator

response: She doesn’t, quite. But she will want to argue about it, and he wants her to.

At a quarter to eleven Tomás drives him back in the van, the boards in the back clattering every time they go over a dip, the windshield a sheet of water with the wipers barely keeping a hole in it. At the curb Tomás looks over at him for a while, a man weighing what ought to be said at a time like this, and says it. “Point’s closed, bro.”

choices.text: *Say goodnight to her asleep — out loud, in case.*
response: “Goodnight, Skye.”

He says it at a regular volume, to her face, in case some part of her is keeping track. Her eyelids don’t move. But her hand, loose on his knee, closes on a fold of his sweatpants and holds on, and doesn’t let go until he’s got the pillow under her head instead.

At a quarter to eleven Tomás drives him home in the van with the boards rattling in the back and the defroster losing, and doesn’t say anything until the Delgado curb. There he puts it in park and looks out at the rain coming down on the empty quad, personally let down by it. “Point’s closed, bro.”

body: Giorgio’s windows have run down to the sills with rain and steam, so that Mission Street outside is only a smear of red brake lights and the green cross on the pharmacy, and the light in here comes from the little lamps over the booths, low and orange on the checkered oilcloth. It’s nearly empty. Everybody with sense is home.

They have the back booth and a large pie, half pepperoni and half plain, because she’s a purist about nothing in the world but this. She sits sideways with her back against the wall and her wet sneakers up on the bench, in his flannel again, with *Oceanography 1* open on her knees. He has a Giorgio’s pen and a placemat — a map of Italy, the regions in five colors, a cartoon chef in a toque standing in Calabria where Nonna’s from — turned over to its blank side, because his legal pad is in 412 and the three pages are due at one.
Three pages on why you are wrong. Frankenstein; the trial; the girl they hang; the silence. He has to find the sentence that starts it.

“Welcome,” Skye says, in a voice like a carpeted hallway, “to Chapter Four.” She turns the book to an imaginary group behind her. “Please stay together. Please do not touch the waves. You are now standing in front of a wave. Notice the crest. Notice the trough. The trough is the low part. The artist has made the trough low as a comment on the human condition.” She turns a page. “If you’ll follow me into the next gallery, we’ll see what happens when a wave reaches shallow water. I won’t spoil it. It breaks. Press seven on your keypad for the gift shop.”

He writes the first sentence and crosses it out. He writes the second. She goes on through the galleries — the period, the fetch, the wave of translation, which she says is the wave’s *late period*, when it stopped caring what critics thought — and he writes under it, a paragraph, then most of another, eating crusts off the plain half without looking. The rain keeps coming down the window beside them.

When he stops to read it over she leans across the pizza and reads it upside down. She reads slowly, with her lips almost moving. Then she puts one finger, greasy at the tip, on one sentence. Not the first. Not the clever one.
“That one,” she says. “That’s the one you actually think. The rest is you doing Hale.”
He looks at the sentence under her finger. It’s the one he almost didn’t write down.

She sits back against the wall and takes another slice, and folds it in half, New York, which she does to irritate the waiter. “Friday,” she says. “Conan’s last show. My house. I’m going to be awake for it.”
“Friday.”
“I’m going to make popcorn and cry about a man I’ve never met.” She points the slice at him. “You’re going to hold the bowl.”

choices.text: *Cross out everything but the true sentence.*
response: He draws a line through everything else, sentence by sentence, the clever one first, until there’s one sentence left alive in the middle of the placemat with Italy on the other side of it. Skye watches him do it with her chin on her hand.
“Brutal,” she says, approving. “You’re a butcher.”

At twenty to eleven she drops him at the Delgado curb with the top up and the wipers on high. “Two and three-quarter pages to go,” she says. “Don’t write anything you don’t think.” He goes up the steps with the placemat folded inside his jacket against the rain, and the one sentence on it.

She’s already in the voice; she lifts the placemat off the oilcloth like a piece in a case. “You are now standing in front of a young man who would like to be finished,” she says, in the carpet voice. “He has been standing here for some time. Notice the pen. Notice the crust he has not eaten. The artist —”
“Skye.”
“The artist would like to be left alone,” says the guide, and hands it back, and takes the crust.

At twenty to eleven she drops him at Delgado with the top up and the rain coming off the canvas in ropes. “Notice the pages,” she says, through the window, in the voice. “Notice that there are three of them. Tomorrow.” He goes up the steps laughing, with the placemat buttoned inside his jacket.

He folds it in four, carefully, along Italy’s borders, with the grease spot from her finger on the true sentence, and puts it in the inside pocket of the Carhartt. She watches him do it, and doesn’t say anything clever, and then she does.
“You’re keeping a placemat,” she says. “Of me being right.”
“That’s why.”

At twenty to eleven she drops him at the Delgado curb with the top up. He gets out into the rain with his hand on his jacket over the pocket, to keep it dry, and she leans across the passenger seat to the open door. “Write the rest of it like that one,” she says. And then he shuts the door on her, because it’s raining in on the seat.
